title: Symbols and Well-Known Symbols
summary: Create unique property keys and customize certain built-in language behaviors.
nestedConcepts: Use well-known symbols as language hooks

subtopics.title: Create unique symbols
subtopics.explanation: Calling `Symbol()` creates a unique primitive value, even when two symbols have the same description. Symbols are often used as property keys when a library needs a key unlikely to collide with a string property. The description helps debugging; it does not determine identity.

subtopics.title: Find symbol-keyed properties
subtopics.explanation: Symbol-keyed properties are skipped by common string-key tools such as `Object.keys()` and `for...in`. They are not truly private: code can discover them with `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols()` or `Reflect.ownKeys()`. Use `#private` fields when you need class-enforced privacy.

subtopics.title: Share symbols with Symbol.for()
subtopics.explanation: `Symbol.for(key)` looks up a symbol in a shared global registry and creates one if needed. Calling it again with the same key returns the same symbol. Use it only when separate parts of an application intentionally need a shared key; ordinary `Symbol()` calls are safer for local uniqueness.

subtopics.title: Use well-known symbols as language hooks
subtopics.explanation: JavaScript provides well-known symbols that let objects customize built-in behavior. For example, `Symbol.iterator` identifies the method used by `for...of`. These hooks are advanced extension points; implement one when an object should work naturally with a language feature, not just to hide a method name.

subtopics.title: Distinguish symbols from private fields
subtopics.explanation: A symbol key reduces accidental name collisions, but other code can still discover it. A class field written as `#value` is private to the class body and cannot be accessed through reflection. Choose a symbol for an unusual public key and `#private` for enforced class privacy.

foundations.overview: A Symbol is a unique primitive value often used as a property key. Even symbols with the same description are different values. Well-known symbols are shared built-in keys that let objects customize behaviors such as iteration.
foundations.mentalModel: A symbol is like a one-of-a-kind key with a label written on it.
foundations.whyItMatters: Symbols can avoid accidental key collisions in shared objects and libraries.

keyTakeaways: A symbol property does not appear in ordinary string-key enumeration.
Symbol.for uses a shared global registry.
Well-known symbols define hooks used by JavaScript features.
Private class fields use a different # syntax.
